Formulas to Memorize

Preferences & Utility tab 1 →
MRS (slope of the indifference curve)
$$\text{MRS} = \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{u} = -\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}$$
Negative. $|\text{MRS}|$ = units of $y$ given up for one more $x$.
Cobb–Douglas MRS
$$u = x^\alpha y^\beta \;\Rightarrow\; \text{MRS} = -\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\,\frac{y}{x}$$
Only the exponent ratio matters.
Same preferences?
$$V = f(u),\ f' > 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{same MRS}$$
$\ln u,\ u^2,\ 3u+5$ yes; $-u,\ 1/u$ no.
Homothetic test
$$\text{MRS}(tx, ty) = \text{MRS}(x, y)$$
MRS depends only on $y/x$. Quasilinear fails.
Diminishing MRS
$$|\text{MRS}| \downarrow \text{ as } x \uparrow \text{ along one curve}$$
Curve flattens ⇒ convex preferences.
Convexity (weak)
$$A \succsim C,\ B \succsim C \Rightarrow tA + (1-t)B \succsim C$$
Averages beat extremes; test with a numeric average.
Budget & Demand tab 2 →
Budget: income / endowment
$$p_x x + p_y y = M \quad\text{or}\quad = p_x\omega_x + p_y\omega_y$$
Slope $-p_x/p_y$. Endowment line always passes through $\omega$.
Tangency (smooth optimum)
$$\text{MRS} = -\frac{p_x}{p_y} \iff \frac{MU_x}{MU_y} = \frac{p_x}{p_y}$$
Then substitute into the budget.
Cobb–Douglas demand
$$x^* = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\frac{M}{p_x},\qquad y^* = \frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\frac{M}{p_y}$$
Fixed spending shares.
Perfect substitutes $ax + by$ (bang per buck)
$$\frac{MU_x}{p_x} = \frac{a}{p_x}\ \ \text{vs}\ \ \frac{MU_y}{p_y} = \frac{b}{p_y}$$
Spend everything on the bigger one: $x^* = M/p_x$ or $y^* = M/p_y$. Equal ⇒ any point on the budget line.
Perfect complements $\min\{ax, by\}$
$$ax = by:\quad x^* = \frac{bM}{bp_x + ap_y},\quad y^* = \frac{aM}{bp_x + ap_y}$$
Kink plus budget; never differentiate.
Quasilinear $v(x) + \beta y$
$$\text{MRS} = -\frac{v'(x)}{\beta},\qquad v'(x^*) = \beta\frac{p_x}{p_y},\qquad y^* = \frac{M - p_x x^*}{p_y}\ (\ge 0)$$
$x^*$ ignores income. Usually $\beta = 1$.
Net demand & autarky
$$\begin{gathered} z_x = x^* - \omega_x \\ \text{autarky: } x^*(p) = \omega_x,\ \ -p = \text{MRS}(\omega)\end{gathered}$$
$z_x > 0$ buyer, $< 0$ seller.
Homogeneity of degree 0
$$x^*(tp_x, tp_y, tM) = x^*(p_x, p_y, M)$$
So normalize $p_y = 1$, $p_x = p$.
Exchange Economy tab 3 →
Feasible
$$x_1 + x_2 \le X,\qquad y_1 + y_2 \le Y$$
Box is $X$ by $Y$; $x_2 = X - x_1$.
Pareto dominates
$$u_i(Z) \ge u_i(W)\ \forall i,\quad u_j(Z) > u_j(W) \text{ some } j$$
Never add utilities.
Pareto optimal (interior)
$$\text{MRS}_A = \text{MRS}_B$$
Leontief: on the kink ray. Linear vs linear: edges.
Lens & core
$$\begin{gathered}\text{lens: } u_A \ge u_A(\omega)\ \text{and}\ u_B \ge u_B(\omega)\\ \text{core} = \text{contract curve} \cap \text{lens}\end{gathered}$$
Endpoints: solve $u_i(\text{CC}) = u_i(\omega)$.
$B$ in $A$’s coordinates
$$x_B = X - x_A,\qquad y_B = Y - y_A$$
Substitute before setting MRSs equal.
Cobb–Douglas contract curve
$$y_A = \frac{r_B\,Y\,x_A}{r_A X - (r_A - r_B)x_A},\quad r_i = \frac{\alpha_i}{\beta_i}$$
Diagonal iff $r_A = r_B$.

Box Match: Preferences → Edgeworth Box

Nine boxes, nine pairs of preferences. Each box shows the endowment (dot), the two indifference curves through it, the lens (shaded), the contract curve (gold) and the core (dark). Drag each preference tile onto the box it produces — or tap a tile, then tap a box. Tap a placed tile to send it back.

Ask yourself: are the curves smooth, straight, or L-shaped? Does the Pareto set run through the middle, along a kink ray, or along the edges? Which person values $x$ more, and which edges does that pick out?

Matched: 0 / 9

Preference tiles

Shape rules to lean on

  • Both smooth (Cobb–Douglas): a curve from corner to corner where $\text{MRS}_A = \text{MRS}_B$.
  • One Leontief: the Pareto set is that person’s kink ray — and it stops where the ray exits the box.
  • Both Leontief, same ratio: the diagonal if the totals are in the ratio; otherwise a parallelogram band between the two kink rays.
  • Smooth vs linear: a ray through the origin ($\text{MRS}$ = the constant), then along the edge it hits.
  • Linear vs linear, different slopes: two edges — whoever values $x$ more ends up with all of it (their far edge), or the other person holds all the $y$.
  • Linear vs linear, same slope: the whole box; the lens collapses to the shared line through $\omega$.
  • Quasilinear $v(x)+y$ vs linear: a vertical line at the $x$ that solves $v'(x) = $ the constant.

Study guide, part 1 of 3. How preferences are described, what the axioms buy you, why utility is only a ranking, and everything about the MRS. Memorize-list and flashcards live on the ★ Cheat Sheet.

1

Preferences & the Axioms

Notation. $A \succsim B$: “$A$ is at least as good as $B$” (weak preference).  $A \succ B$: strictly better.  $A \sim B$: indifferent. A rational preference relation is one that is complete and transitive — those two are the non-negotiables; the rest give indifference curves their familiar shape.

AxiomStatementWhat it buys you on the graphViolated by…
CompletenessFor any two bundles, $A \succsim B$ or $B \succsim A$ (or both). You can always rank.Every bundle sits on some indifference curve — the map covers the whole space.“I can’t compare those.”
Transitivity$A \succsim B$ and $B \succsim C \Rightarrow A \succsim C$.Indifference curves cannot cross.$A \succ B \succ C \succ A$ (a cycle) — no utility function can represent this.
ContinuityNo sudden jumps: if $A \succ B$, bundles very close to $A$ are still preferred to bundles very close to $B$.Curves are unbroken lines; needed for a utility function to exist.Lexicographic preferences (rank by $x$ first, use $y$ only to break ties).
MonotonicityWeak: more of every good is at least as good. Strong (strict): more of any good, no less of the others, is strictly better. (“More is better” — goods, not bads.)Curves slope down; curves farther from the origin are better; curves are thin.Bads (pollution); satiation (bliss point). $\min\{x,y\}$ is weakly but not strictly monotone.
ConvexityWeak: if $A \succsim C$ and $B \succsim C$ then $tA + (1-t)B \succsim C$ for $t\in[0,1]$. Strict: $\succ$ whenever $A \ne B$, $0<t<1$. “Averages are at least as good as extremes.”Curves bow toward the origin; $|\text{MRS}|$ diminishes along a curve; the tangency is the unique optimum.$u = x^2 + y^2$ (curves bow away; the consumer specializes). Perfect substitutes are weakly but not strictly convex.

Theory questions you could be asked

Each card is a question in the professor’s voice, a model answer, and a worked example behind the button. Practice by covering the answer.

QWhy must indifference curves slope downward?

Monotonicity. Moving up-right adds both goods, so the new bundle is strictly better — it cannot be on the same curve. To stay indifferent after gaining $x$, the consumer must give up some $y$; hence the curve falls.

$u = xy$ through $(2,8)$, so $u = 16$. Gain one $x$: $(3, y)$ is on the same curve only if $3y = 16 \Rightarrow y = 5.33$. Two more: $(5, 3.2)$. Every step right is a step down — the curve $y = 16/x$ is decreasing.

QProve that two indifference curves cannot cross. Name the axioms you use.

Suppose curves 1 and 2 cross at $A$. Pick $B$ on curve 1 and $C$ on curve 2 with $C$ containing more of both goods than $B$. By monotonicity, $C \succ B$. But $A \sim B$ and $A \sim C$, so by transitivity $B \sim C$. Contradiction — the curves never cross.

Let curve 1 be $xy = 36$ and suppose a second curve also passes through $A = (6,6)$ but is steeper, so that at $x = 8$ it sits at $C = (8, 5)$ while curve 1 sits at $B = (8, 4.5)$. $C$ has more $y$ than $B$ and the same $x$ ⇒ $C \succ B$ (monotonicity). Yet both are indifferent to $A$ ⇒ $B \sim C$ (transitivity). Impossible, so the second curve cannot pass through $A$.

QWhat does it mean for preferences to be convex? Show whether $u = x^2 + y^2$ is convex.

Averages are at least as good as extremes: if $A \succsim C$ and $B \succsim C$ then any mix $tA + (1-t)B \succsim C$. Equivalently the better-than set (everything on or above a curve) is a convex set, so curves bow toward the origin. Test: take two bundles on one curve, average them, compare.

$u = x^2 + y^2$: $(4,0)$ and $(0,4)$ both give $16$; their average $(2,2)$ gives $8$ — strictly worse. Not convex (curves are quarter-circles bowed away from the origin; the consumer specializes in one good).
Contrast $u = xy$: $(1,9)$ and $(9,1)$ give $9$; $(5,5)$ gives $25$ — better. Strictly convex.
Contrast $u = x + y$: $(4,0)$, $(0,4)$ and $(2,2)$ all give $4$ — equal. Weakly but not strictly convex.

QDistinguish weak and strict monotonicity. Which does $u = \min\{x,y\}$ satisfy?

Weak: more of every good is at least as good. Strict: more of any one good (no less of the others) is strictly better. $\min\{x,y\}$ is weakly monotone (more of both never hurts) but not strictly (extra of one good alone can be idle).

At $(3,3)$, $u = 3$. Raise $x$ to $4$: $u = \min\{4,3\} = 3$ — no gain, so strict fails. Raise both to $(4,4)$: $u = 4$ — weak holds.
$u = xy$: $\partial u/\partial x = y > 0$ on the interior, so strict holds there; on the axis $y = 0$, raising $x$ leaves $u = 0$ (only weak) — which is why Cobb–Douglas curves never touch the axes.

QWhich two axioms make preferences “rational”, and what goes wrong without each?

Completeness and transitivity. Without completeness some pairs can’t be ranked, so some bundles have no indifference curve. Without transitivity you can get a cycle $A \succ B \succ C \succ A$, which no utility function can represent (it would need $u(A) > u(B) > u(C) > u(A)$).

A student says pizza $\succ$ sushi, sushi $\succ$ tacos, tacos $\succ$ pizza. Try assigning numbers: pizza $= 3$, sushi $= 2$, tacos $= 1$ — but then tacos $\succ$ pizza needs $1 > 3$. Every assignment fails, so transitivity is the violated axiom and the preferences have no utility representation.

2

Utility Is Ordinal: Monotonic Transformations

Definition. $u$ represents $\succsim$ if $u(A) \ge u(B) \iff A \succsim B$. Only the ranking carries information: $u=10$ vs $u=5$ does not mean “twice as happy”, and utility numbers cannot be compared across people — which is exactly why welfare on the Exchange tab uses the Pareto criterion instead of adding utilities.

Positive monotonic transformation

$V = f(u)$ with $f'(u) > 0$ represents the same preferences: the ranking of every pair is preserved.

Same preferences: $\ln u$, $u^2$ (for $u \ge 0$), $\sqrt u$, $e^{u}$, $3u$, $u+5$, $5u+2$.

Not the same: $-u$, $1/u$, $(u-5)^2$ — these reverse or scramble the ranking somewhere.

Fast test: compare the MRS

$$\text{MRS}_V = -\frac{f'(u)\,MU_x}{f'(u)\,MU_y} = \text{MRS}_u$$

The $f'(u)$ cancels (chain rule), so same MRS function $\Rightarrow$ same indifference map. Different MRS $\Rightarrow$ different preferences.

The log trick (Cobb–Douglas)

$u = x^\alpha y^\beta \;\Rightarrow\; \ln u = \alpha\ln x + \beta \ln y$ — same preferences, easier derivatives. Exponents can be rescaled: $x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}$ and $x^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)}y^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)}$ are the same preferences. Only the ratio $\alpha/\beta$ matters.

Writing $u(x,y)$ from a description

  • “Only cares about total sugar; $x$ has 3× the sugar of $y$” → $u = 3x + y$.
  • “Enjoys 3 espressos with 2 cakes” → $u = \min\{2x, 3y\}$ (coefficients swapped so $2x = 3y$ at the ideal ratio $x{:}y = 3{:}2$).
  • “2 glasses of apple ($y$) = 1 glass of orange ($x$)” → $u = 2x + y$.

Twelve more of these, with checks and a timer, on the ⚡ Sprint tab.

QShow that $V = xy$ and $W = 5xy + 2$ represent the same preferences as $u = \ln x + \ln y$.

$V = e^{u}$ and $W = 5e^{u} + 2$ are both increasing functions of $u$ (positive monotonic transformations), so every ranking is preserved. Confirm with the MRS: all three give $\text{MRS} = -y/x$.

$u$: $MU_x = 1/x$, $MU_y = 1/y$ ⇒ $\text{MRS} = -\dfrac{1/x}{1/y} = -\dfrac{y}{x}$.  $V$: $-\dfrac{y}{x}$.  $W$: $-\dfrac{5y}{5x} = -\dfrac{y}{x}$. Identical MRS everywhere ⇒ identical indifference curves. Counter-example: $T = 1/(xy) = e^{-u}$ is decreasing in $u$ — same curves, reversed ranking, different preferences.

QA classmate says allocation $B$ has total utility 20 and $A$ has 18, so $B$ is better for society. Give two reasons this is wrong.

(1) Utility is ordinal: each person’s number can be rescaled by any increasing transformation, so a sum across people is meaningless. (2) Welfare comparisons in this course are person-by-person (Pareto): $B$ beats $A$ only if nobody is worse off and someone is better off.

Consumer 1: $u_1 = xy$, consumer 2: $u_2 = x + y$. At $A$ utilities are $(9, 9)$, total $18$; at $B$ they are $(4, 16)$, total $20$. Consumer 1 is worse off at $B$, so $B$ does not Pareto dominate $A$. Now relabel consumer 1’s utility as $u_1^2$: $A$ becomes $(81, 9)$ and the “total” flips to $90$ vs $32$ — the sum depended on an arbitrary choice of scale.

3

Marginal Utility & the MRS

Definition

$$MU_x = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x},\qquad \text{MRS}_{xy} = \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{u\text{ const}} = -\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}$$

The MRS is the slope of the indifference curve — a negative number. Its magnitude $|\text{MRS}| = MU_x/MU_y$ is how many units of $y$ the consumer gives up for one more unit of $x$ while staying indifferent.

Derivation: along a curve $du = MU_x\,dx + MU_y\,dy = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{MU_x}{MU_y}$. The minus sign is the “give up $y$”.

Where the MRS shows up

  • Optimum (tangency): $\text{MRS} = -\dfrac{p_x}{p_y}$, i.e. $\dfrac{MU_x}{MU_y} = \dfrac{p_x}{p_y}$.
  • Pareto optimality: $\text{MRS}_A = \text{MRS}_B$ (the two curves are tangent).
  • Gains from trade: if $|\text{MRS}_A| > |\text{MRS}_B|$, $A$ values $x$ more — $A$ buys $x$ from $B$ at any rate in between.
  • Same preferences? Same MRS function.

Cobb–Douglas $x^\alpha y^\beta$: $\text{MRS} = -\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}\dfrac{y}{x}$.

Theory questions you could be asked

QDo these preferences exhibit diminishing MRS? Explain.

Diminishing MRS means $|\text{MRS}|$ falls as you move right along one indifference curve ($x\uparrow$, $y\downarrow$): the curve flattens. Test: write $|\text{MRS}|$ and see whether $x\uparrow$ with $y\downarrow$ pushes it down. It is the calculus face of convexity.

$u = 2xy$: $MU_x = 2y$, $MU_y = 2x$, $\text{MRS} = -y/x$. Along $xy = 36$: at $(2,18)$, $\text{MRS} = -9$; at $(6,6)$, $-1$; at $(18,2)$, $-1/9$. The magnitude falls $9 \to 1 \to 1/9$ ⇒ diminishing MRS. ✓
$u = 3x + y$: $\text{MRS} = -3$ everywhere — constant, not diminishing.
$u = \ln x + y$: $\text{MRS} = -1/x$; as $x$ rises the magnitude falls ⇒ diminishing, even though it never depends on $y$.

QAre these preferences homothetic? Explain.

Homothetic means the MRS depends only on the ratio $y/x$: scaling a bundle by $t$ leaves the MRS unchanged, $\text{MRS}(tx,ty) = \text{MRS}(x,y)$, so the slope is constant along any ray from the origin. Consequence: demand scales with income (double $M$, double both quantities; expenditure shares fixed).

$u = 2xy$: $\text{MRS}(tx,ty) = -\dfrac{ty}{tx} = -\dfrac{y}{x}$ ⇒ homothetic. ✓ (All Cobb–Douglas, perfect substitutes, perfect complements are.)
$u = \ln x + y$: $\text{MRS}(tx,ty) = -\dfrac{1}{tx} \ne -\dfrac{1}{x}$ ⇒ not homothetic. At $(1,1)$ the slope is $-1$; at $(2,2)$, on the same ray, it is $-1/2$.

QWhat is special about quasilinear preferences $u = v(x) + y$?

$\text{MRS} = -v'(x)$ contains no $y$, so every indifference curve is a vertical copy of every other. Demand for $x$ does not depend on income (once interior); $y$ absorbs whatever is left. Not homothetic.

$u = \ln x + y$, $p_y = 1$, $p_x = p$. Tangency $-1/x = -p \Rightarrow x^* = 1/p$ whatever the income. With $M = 10$: $y^* = 10 - 1$; with $M = 20$: $y^* = 20 - 1$; $x^*$ stays at $1/p$. Curves: $y = c - \ln x$ for each level $c$ — the same shape, shifted up.

Sanity checks on any demand function. (1) Plug back into the budget: $p_x x^* + p_y y^* = M$. (2) Scale every price and $M$ by the same factor: nothing should change (homogeneous of degree zero). (3) $x^*$ should fall in $p_x$ (except perfect substitutes at the switch point).

2

Budget Lines: Money Income vs. Endowment

Money income $M$

$$p_x x + p_y y = M,\qquad \text{slope } = -\frac{p_x}{p_y},\qquad \text{intercepts } \frac{M}{p_x},\ \frac{M}{p_y}$$

$M\uparrow$: parallel shift out. $p_x\uparrow$: pivots inward around the $y$-intercept. Intercepts first, then connect.

Endowment $\omega = (\omega_x, \omega_y)$

$$p_x x + p_y y = p_x \omega_x + p_y \omega_y \;(= M)$$

Income is the market value of what you own, so it moves with prices. The line always passes through $\omega$; a price change pivots it around $\omega$, not around an intercept.

Net demand $z_x = x^* - \omega_x$: positive = net buyer, negative = net seller. Value of what you sell = value of what you buy.

Homogeneity of degree zero

Multiply $p_x$, $p_y$ and $M$ all by $t$: the budget set is unchanged, so demand is unchanged (HW1 Q2e). With an endowment, scaling prices alone is enough, because income scales automatically.

Hence only the relative price $p = p_x/p_y$ matters ⇒ it is legal to normalize $p_y = 1$, $p_x = p$.

Autarky price

The price at which the consumer chooses exactly $\omega$: solve $x^*(p) = \omega_x$. At that price $-p = \text{MRS}(\omega)$ — the budget line is tangent to the indifference curve through the endowment.

Below the autarky price the consumer buys $x$; above it, sells $x$.

3

Algorithm: Marshallian Demand (UMP)

Cover the right column and run the left yourself. Running example is HW1 Q3: $u = 2xy$, endowment $(5, 10)$.

General move
Running example

1Givens. Write $u$, prices, and the budget (money income or endowment form).

$u = 2xy$; budget $p_x x + p_y y = 5p_x + 10p_y$.

2Classify the function (Section 1 of this tab). Smooth → tangency. Substitutes → bang per buck $MU_x/p_x$ vs $MU_y/p_y$, corner. Complements → ratio. Quasilinear → tangency then check $y\ge0$.

Cobb–Douglas ($\alpha=\beta=1$) → tangency. (The 2 is a monotonic transformation of $xy$; ignore it.)

3MRS. $\text{MRS} = -MU_x / MU_y$, simplified.

$MU_x = 2y,\ MU_y = 2x \Rightarrow \text{MRS} = -y/x$.

4Tangency. $\text{MRS} = -p_x/p_y$ (the minus signs cancel) — solve for one variable in terms of the other.

$-y/x = -p_x/p_y \Rightarrow p_y y = p_x x$.

5Substitute into the budget and solve for $x^*$, then $y^*$.

$p_x x + p_x x = 5p_x + 10p_y \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{5p_x + 10p_y}{2p_x} = \dfrac{5}{2} + \dfrac{5p_y}{p_x}$,  $y^* = \dfrac{5p_x + 10p_y}{2p_y} = \dfrac{5p_x}{2p_y} + 5$.

6Normalize if asked ($p_y = 1,\ p_x = p$) and check the budget.

$x^* = \tfrac52 + \tfrac{5}{p},\ \ y^* = \tfrac{5p}{2} + 5$. Check: $p x^* + y^* = \tfrac{5p}{2} + 5 + \tfrac{5p}{2} + 5 = 5p + 10$. ✓

7Interpret. Net buyer or seller? Autarky price?

$x^* = 5 \iff p = 2$ (autarky). For $p < 2$ she buys $x$; for $p > 2$ she sells $x$. Note $\text{MRS}(5,10) = -10/5 = -2 = -p$. ✓

Lagrangian version (same thing). $\mathcal L = u(x,y) - \lambda\,(p_x x + p_y y - M)$. FOCs: $MU_x = \lambda p_x$, $MU_y = \lambda p_y$ ⇒ $\dfrac{MU_x}{p_x} = \dfrac{MU_y}{p_y}$ (“equal bang per buck”) ⇒ $\dfrac{MU_x}{MU_y} = \dfrac{p_x}{p_y}$. $\lambda$ = marginal utility of income.

Study guide, part 3 of 3. Two consumers, one box: feasibility, Pareto dominance, the contract curve by preference type, then the decision tree and the traps. Memorize-list and flashcards live on the ★ Cheat Sheet.

1

Exchange Economy: Feasibility, Pareto, the Box

TermPrecise definitionHow to check it
Endowment / totalsEach consumer starts with $\omega_i = (\omega_{ix}, \omega_{iy})$. Totals: $X = \omega_{1x}+\omega_{2x}$, $Y = \omega_{1y}+\omega_{2y}$.The box is $X$ wide and $Y$ tall.
AllocationA list of bundles $\{(x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)\}$, one per consumer.One point in the box fixes both bundles: $x_2 = X - x_1$, $y_2 = Y - y_1$.
FeasibleUses no more than the totals: $x_1 + x_2 \le X$, $y_1 + y_2 \le Y$ (with equality when nothing is thrown away).Add up each good.
Pareto dominates$Z$ Pareto dominates $W$ if every consumer is at least as well off at $Z$ and at least one is strictly better off. (Strict version: everyone strictly better.)Compare utilities consumer-by-consumer. “$u_1$ up, $u_2$ down” = neither dominates. Never add utilities.
Pareto optimal (efficient)Feasible, and no feasible allocation Pareto dominates it: you cannot help one person without hurting another.Interior with smooth ICs: $\text{MRS}_1 = \text{MRS}_2$. Otherwise: look for idle goods or a mutually beneficial trade — if you find one, not PO.
Contract curve / Pareto setThe set of all Pareto-optimal allocations in the box. Always runs from $O_1$ to $O_2$.Section 2 below.
LensAllocations that Pareto-dominate $\omega$: $u_1 \ge u_1(\omega)$ and $u_2 \ge u_2(\omega)$. Bounded by the two ICs through $\omega$.Draw both ICs through $\omega$; shade between them.
Core (“PO relative to the endowment”)Pareto-optimal and in the lens. Where voluntary trade from $\omega$ can end up.Intersect the contract curve with the lens: solve $u_1(\text{CC}) = u_1(\omega)$ and $u_2(\text{CC}) = u_2(\omega)$ for the two endpoints.
$A$’s origin bottom-left, $B$’s top-right; $B$’s axes read backwards. Lens shaded; contract curve gold; core = the dark segment.

Why unequal MRS means gains from trade

Say $\text{MRS}_A = -3$ and $\text{MRS}_B = -1$. $A$ would give up to $3y$ for one $x$; $B$ would accept as little as $1y$. Any price between $1$ and $3$ makes both strictly better off $\Rightarrow$ the allocation is not PO.

Direction: the person with the larger $|\text{MRS}|$ buys $x$ (they value it more) and pays in $y$.

Two tricks for finding a Pareto improvement

  • Idle-goods trick (Leontief present): if $u = \min\{x, 2y\}$ and the consumer holds $(4,4)$, only $2$ units of $y$ are used — hand the other $2$ to anyone with monotone preferences. They gain, the Leontief consumer loses nothing.
  • MRS-gap trick (smooth): move a small amount of $x$ from the low-$|\text{MRS}|$ person to the high-$|\text{MRS}|$ person and pay back $y$ at a rate strictly between the two.

Recipe for “does $B$ Pareto dominate $A$?” (HW2 type)

  1. Feasibility: add up each good at each allocation.
  2. Compute every consumer’s utility at every allocation (Leontief: take the min; note which good is idle).
  3. Compare consumer-by-consumer: all $\ge$ and one $>$? Then yes. Any $<$? Then no.
  4. Write the sentence with the exact words: “$B$ Pareto dominates $A$ because consumer 1 is no worse off ($u_1$: 4 → 4) and consumer 2 is strictly better off ($u_2$: 10 → 12).”
  5. Explain the trade: who gives up what, and why it hurts nobody (idle units, or MRS gap).

Reading B’s indifference curve in A’s coordinates

Substitute $x_B = X - x_A,\ y_B = Y - y_A$ into $u_B$. E.g. $u_B = x_B + 2y_B$ through $\omega$ with $u_B(\omega) = 8$ in a $4\times4$ box: $(4-x_A) + 2(4-y_A) = 8 \Rightarrow x_A + 2y_A = 4$.

$B$ gains when $A$ holds less, so $B$’s better-off side is toward $O_A$: $u_B \ge 8 \iff x_A + 2y_A \le 4$.

2

Algorithm: the Contract Curve

Running example (from the Exchange GE sheet): $u_A = x_A^{3/4}y_A^{1/4}$, $u_B = x_B^{1/4}y_B^{3/4}$, $\omega_A = (4,8)$, $\omega_B = (8,4)$, so $X = Y = 12$.

General move
Running example

1Box & coordinates. Totals $X, Y$. Write $B$’s bundle as $(X - x_A,\ Y - y_A)$ so everything lives in $A$’s coordinates.

$X = 12,\ Y = 12$; $x_B = 12 - x_A,\ y_B = 12 - y_A$.

2Both MRSs, each in its own variables, then substitute $B$’s.

$\text{MRS}_A = -\dfrac{3/4}{1/4}\dfrac{y_A}{x_A} = -\dfrac{3y_A}{x_A}$;  $\text{MRS}_B = -\dfrac{1/4}{3/4}\dfrac{y_B}{x_B} = -\dfrac{12 - y_A}{3(12 - x_A)}$.

3Set equal (interior tangency): $\text{MRS}_A = \text{MRS}_B$. The minus signs cancel.

$\dfrac{3y_A}{x_A} = \dfrac{12 - y_A}{3(12-x_A)}$.

4Cross-multiply and solve for $y_A$ as a function of $x_A$.

$9y_A(12 - x_A) = x_A(12 - y_A) \Rightarrow 108y_A - 9x_Ay_A = 12x_A - x_Ay_A \Rightarrow 108 y_A - 8x_Ay_A = 12x_A$ ⇒ $y_A = \dfrac{12x_A}{108 - 8x_A} = \dfrac{3x_A}{27 - 2x_A}$.

5Endpoint check. It must pass through $(0,0)$ and $(X,Y)$. Say which side of the diagonal it lies on and why.

$x_A=0 \Rightarrow y_A=0$ ✓; $x_A = 12 \Rightarrow y_A = 36/3 = 12$ ✓. At $x_A=6$: $y_A = 18/15 = 1.2 < 6$ → below the diagonal ($A$ likes $x$ relatively more, so along the curve $A$ holds relatively more $x$).

6Non-smooth cases: replace step 3 with the case rules below (kink ray, corner/edge, band).

Both smooth here — nothing to clip.

7Core. Intersect with the lens: solve $u_A(x_A, y_A(x_A)) = u_A(\omega)$ and $u_B(\ldots) = u_B(\omega)$ for the two endpoints.

Endpoints come from $x_A^{3/4}y_A^{1/4} = 4^{3/4}8^{1/4}$ and the $B$ analogue along $y_A = 3x_A/(27-2x_A)$ (numeric: $x_A \approx 6.89$ to $10.44$).

General Cobb–Douglas contract curve. With $u_i = x_i^{\alpha_i}y_i^{\beta_i}$ and $r_i = \alpha_i/\beta_i$:

$$y_A = \frac{r_B\,Y\,x_A}{r_A X - (r_A - r_B)\,x_A}$$   It is the diagonal exactly when $r_A = r_B$ (identical relative tastes); below the diagonal when $r_A > r_B$.

Contract-curve shapes by preference type (HW3’s four problems)

PairPareto setReasoning in one line
Smooth vs smooth (both CD)A curve from $O_A$ to $O_B$ where $\text{MRS}_A = \text{MRS}_B$.Tangency of the two indifference curves.
Smooth vs linear (HW3 Q1: $xy$ vs $3x+y$)Ray $\text{MRS}_A = -3 \Rightarrow y_A = 3x_A$ from $O_A$ until it hits an edge, then along that edge to $O_B$.Interior: $A$’s MRS must equal $B$’s constant. On the edge $B$ holds only one good, so no trade can help $B$ without hurting $A$.
Leontief vs anything monotone (HW3 Q2: $\min\{2x,y\}$ vs $x+y$)The Leontief consumer’s kink ray $y_1 = 2x_1$, clipped to the box.Off the ray consumer 1 has an idle good — give it away (not PO). On the ray, any change lowers 1’s min. Beyond where the ray exits the box (top edge), 1 has idle $x$ → not PO.
Linear vs linear, different slopes (HW3 Q3: $2x+y$ vs $x+2y$)Two edges: the person who values $x$ more holds all the $x$ (right edge, $x_1 = X$) or the other person holds all the $y$ (bottom edge, $y_1 = 0$).Whenever 1 still has $y$ and 2 still has $x$, they can swap at a rate between the two $|\text{MRS}|$s.
Leontief vs Leontief, same ratio (HW3 Q4: both $\min\{2x,y\}$)If the total endowment is not in the 1:2 ratio, the Pareto set is the whole band between the two kink rays $y_1 = 2x_1$ and $y_1 = 2x_1 - (2X - Y)$; if it is, the diagonal.The scarce good ($y$, since $Y < 2X$) is fully used by both exactly when $u_1 + u_2 = Y$; that holds anywhere between the rays. Off the band someone has idle $y$.
Linear vs linear, same slopeEvery allocation is PO.Identical MRS everywhere: no mutually beneficial trade exists.
3

Decision Tree & Traps

Which model?

“Write a utility function for…” → classify the story (substitutes / complements / CD / quasilinear), then the Sprint-tab patterns.
One consumer, prices given? → UMP (Budget & Demand tab, §3). First classify the function (Budget & Demand tab, §1). Endowment mentioned? Income $= p\cdot\omega$; finish with net buyer/seller.
“Same preferences?” / “represents” → positive monotonic transformation test or compare MRS (Preferences & Utility tab, §2).
“Convex / homothetic / diminishing MRS?” → the question cards on the Preferences & Utility tab; prove with the MRS formula or a numeric average.
Two consumers, allocations listed? → feasibility → utilities → consumer-by-consumer comparison (Section 1 recipe above).
Two consumers, “contract curve”? → classify both functions, pick the case row (Section 2), then lens and core.

Traps that cost points

  • Adding utilities to judge allocations. Utility is ordinal; Pareto comparisons are person-by-person only.
  • Pareto dominance needs $\ge$ for everyone and $>$ for someone. “One up, one down” is neither.
  • MRS upside down or sign dropped. $\text{MRS} = -MU_x/MU_y$: the slope of the curve, negative, “$y$ given up per $x$”.
  • Perfect substitutes: setting MRS $= -p_x/p_y$. Compare $MU_x/p_x$ with $MU_y/p_y$ instead and go to the corner. Complements: differentiating (use $ax=by$).
  • Endowment budgets: treating $M$ as fixed when prices change. $M = p_x\omega_x + p_y\omega_y$ moves too.
  • Quasilinear: forgetting the $y \ge 0$ check, or thinking $x^*$ depends on income.
  • Contract curve in the wrong coordinates: $B$’s MRS uses $x_B = X - x_A$. Check the curve passes through both origins.
  • Stopping the contract curve where a ray hits an edge: for smooth-vs-linear it continues along the edge; for Leontief it stops (idle good beyond).
  • Calling the whole contract curve the core. Core = contract curve $\cap$ lens.
  • “Convex preferences” vs “convex function”: preferences are convex when the better-than set is convex (curves bow in). $u = x^2+y^2$ is a convex function with non-convex preferences.
  • $u^2$ is a monotonic transformation only when $u \ge 0$; $-u$ and $1/u$ never are.
  • Writing $\min\{3x, 2y\}$ for “3 $x$ per 2 $y$”. The ideal ratio $x{:}y = 3{:}2$ needs $2x = 3y$, i.e. $\min\{2x, 3y\}$.
⚡

Sprint: Story → Utility Function

Twelve descriptions, six minutes. For each one write $u(x,y)$, name the type, and give the MRS (or the kink ratio). Then check, and mark yourself.

Four patterns cover almost everything: substitutes $ax+by$ complements $\min\{ax,by\}$ Cobb–Douglas $x^\alpha y^\beta$ quasilinear $v(x)+y$ — plus two curveballs at the end.

06:00
Score: 0 / 12

How to read a story. “Only cares about the total of…” / “one is worth $k$ of the other” → substitutes. “Uses them together in a fixed ratio” / “$a$ of $x$ with $b$ of $y$” → complements, and the coefficients go on opposite sides: $x{:}y = a{:}b \Rightarrow \min\{bx,\ ay\}$. “Spends a fixed share of income on $x$” → Cobb–Douglas with that share as the exponent. “Extra $y$ is always worth the same, extra $x$ is worth less and less” → quasilinear.

1

Dev only cares about protein. A steak ($x$) has four times the protein of an egg ($y$).

substitutes $u = 4x + y$ (any positive multiple works). $\text{MRS} = -4$: he gives up 4 eggs for a steak. Straight-line curves, slope $-4$.

2

Priya takes exactly two sugar cubes per cup of tea. Cups ($x$), sugar cubes ($y$).

complements $u = \min\{2x,\ y\}$. Ideal ratio $x{:}y = 1{:}2$, kink on the ray $y = 2x$. Sanity check at $(1, 2)$: $\min\{2, 2\}$ — balanced. ✓ The MRS is undefined at the kink (vertical arm $-\infty$, horizontal arm $0$).

3

Leo is indifferent between three apples and one orange. Apples ($x$), oranges ($y$).

substitutes One orange is worth three apples, so $u = x + 3y$ — not $3x + y$. Check: $(3, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ both give $3$. ✓ $\text{MRS} = -1/3$: he gives up only a third of an orange for one more apple.

4

Maya always spends a quarter of her income on books and the rest on clothes, whatever the prices. Books ($x$), clothes ($y$).

Cobb–Douglas Constant expenditure shares are the Cobb–Douglas signature: $u = x^{1/4}y^{3/4}$ (or $xy^3$ — same preferences, ratio $\alpha/\beta = 1/3$). $\text{MRS} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{y}{x}$. Demand: $x^* = \tfrac14 M/p_x$, $y^* = \tfrac34 M/p_y$.

5

Sam builds shelves; each shelf needs four screws and two brackets. Screws ($x$), brackets ($y$). He only cares about finished shelves.

complements Shelves $= \min\{x/4,\ y/2\}$, which is the same preferences as $u = \min\{x,\ 2y\}$ (multiply by 4). Ideal ratio $x{:}y = 4{:}2 = 2{:}1$, kink ray $x = 2y$. Check $(4, 2)$: $\min\{4, 4\}$. ✓ Trap: $\min\{4x, 2y\}$ would say he wants more brackets than screws.

6

Each extra hour of gaming gives Jun the same kick, but each extra coffee gives less and less. Coffee ($x$), gaming hours ($y$).

quasilinear Constant $MU_y$ and diminishing $MU_x$: $u = v(x) + y$ with $v$ concave, e.g. $u = \sqrt{x} + y$ or $u = \ln x + y$. $\text{MRS} = -v'(x)$, e.g. $-\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}$ — no $y$ in it, so the curves are vertical shifts of one another.

7

Omar likes both goods, and a unit of $x$ always gives him twice the satisfaction of a unit of $y$, no matter how much of each he already has.

substitutes Constant marginal utilities in a 2:1 ratio: $u = 2x + y$. $\text{MRS} = -2$. (“No matter how much he already has” is the giveaway for linear preferences.)

8

A recipe needs three cups of flour for every two eggs, and Rosa only cares about how many batches she can make. Flour ($x$), eggs ($y$).

complements $u = \min\{2x,\ 3y\}$. Ratio $x{:}y = 3{:}2$ ⇒ coefficients swap: $2x = 3y$ on the kink ray. Check $(3, 2)$: $\min\{6, 6\}$. ✓ (Batches $= \min\{x/3, y/2\}$, the same preferences.)

9

Ella spends twice as much on $x$ as on $y$ at any prices, and she likes more of both with a smooth, bowed-in indifference map.

Cobb–Douglas Shares $2/3$ on $x$, $1/3$ on $y$: $u = x^{2/3}y^{1/3}$, or equivalently $x^2y$. $\text{MRS} = -\dfrac{2y}{x}$. Demand: $x^* = \tfrac23 M/p_x$, $y^* = \tfrac13 M/p_y$ — spending $\tfrac23 M$ vs $\tfrac13 M$, twice as much. ✓

10

Ravi thinks smoothies and juices are the same drink — he’ll swap one for one without a second thought. Smoothies ($x$), juices ($y$).

substitutes $u = x + y$. $\text{MRS} = -1$. Curves are $45^\circ$ lines; compare $MU_x/p_x = 1/p_x$ with $MU_y/p_y = 1/p_y$ — he buys whichever is cheaper, and is indifferent along the whole budget line if $p_x = p_y$.

11

Curveball: Nadia doesn’t care about $y$ at all — more of it neither helps nor hurts. More $x$ is always better.

neutral good $u = x$ (or $u = 2x$, $\sqrt{x}$…). $MU_y = 0$, so indifference curves are vertical lines: she will not give up any $x$ for $y$ ($|\text{MRS}| \to \infty$). Demand: $x^* = M/p_x$, $y^* = 0$ whenever $p_y > 0$. Monotonicity holds only weakly in $y$.

12

Curveball: Kai likes income ($x$) and dislikes noise ($y$) — each extra decibel costs him as much as one extra dollar helps.

good vs bad $u = x - y$. $MU_y = -1 < 0$, so monotonicity fails in $y$: $y$ is a bad. $\text{MRS} = -\dfrac{MU_x}{MU_y} = -\dfrac{1}{-1} = +1$: indifference curves slope upward — to accept more noise he must be paid more income. “Better” is down-right (more $x$, less $y$).

The pattern table (memorize this, not the twelve answers)

Story says…TypeWriteThen check
“$1$ unit of $x$ is worth $k$ units of $y$” / “only the total of … matters”Perfect substitutes$u = kx + y$$(1,0)$ and $(0,k)$ give the same $u$; $\text{MRS} = -k$.
“$a$ of $x$ goes with $b$ of $y$” (fixed proportions, no substitution)Perfect complements$u = \min\{bx,\ ay\}$ (coefficients swapped)Plug in $(a, b)$: both arguments equal.
“Spends share $s$ of income on $x$” / smooth, bowed-in, likes varietyCobb–Douglas$u = x^{s}y^{1-s}$ (only the exponent ratio matters)$\text{MRS} = -\dfrac{s}{1-s}\dfrac{y}{x}$; shares $s$ and $1-s$.
“Extra $y$ always worth the same; extra $x$ worth less and less”Quasilinear$u = v(x) + y$, $v$ concave ($\sqrt x$, $\ln x$)$\text{MRS} = -v'(x)$ has no $y$.
“Doesn’t care about $y$”Neutral good$u = x$Vertical indifference curves.
“Dislikes $y$”Bad$u = x - ky$Upward-sloping curves; $\text{MRS} > 0$.

A

Mock Test A

Five problems, 100 points, ~75 minutes. Same format as the homework: work on paper, list the givens first, then check each part.

Coverage: P1 axioms & writing utility functions • P2 Cobb–Douglas with an endowment • P3 quasilinear with an endowment • P4 Edgeworth box (smooth vs linear) • P5 Pareto dominance with a Leontief consumer.

1

22 ptsPreferences and the axioms. Short answers; a sentence or two each unless a calculation is asked for.

aState completeness and transitivity in symbols. Which one guarantees that every bundle lies on some indifference curve, and which one rules out crossing curves?

Completeness: for all $A, B$: $A \succsim B$ or $B \succsim A$. Transitivity: $A \succsim B$ and $B \succsim C \Rightarrow A \succsim C$. Completeness gives a ranking of every bundle against every other, so each bundle sits on a curve (the map covers the space). Transitivity (with monotonicity) is what forbids crossing.

bPriya reports: “I prefer $A$ to $B$, $B$ to $C$, and $C$ to $A$.” Which axiom fails? Why can no utility function represent her preferences?

Transitivity fails ($A \succ B \succ C$ should give $A \succ C$, not $C \succ A$). A utility function would need $u(A) > u(B) > u(C) > u(A)$ — impossible for real numbers.

cLet $u(x,y) = x^{1/2}y^{1/2}$. Which of $V = xy$, $W = \tfrac12 \ln x + \tfrac12 \ln y$, $Z = x^{1/2}y^{1/2} - 4$, $T = \dfrac{1}{xy}$ represent the same preferences? Justify each with the phrase “positive monotonic transformation”.

$V = u^2$ (increasing for $u \ge 0$) ✓. $W = \ln u$ (increasing) ✓. $Z = u - 4$ (increasing) ✓. $T = u^{-2}$ is decreasing in $u$ → it reverses every ranking ✗. Quick confirmation: $V, W, Z$ all have $\text{MRS} = -y/x$ like $u$; $T$ gives the same curves but ranks them backwards.

dA consumer has $u = x^2 + y^2$. Compute $u$ at $(4,0)$, $(0,4)$ and at their average $(2,2)$. Are these preferences convex? Sketch the shape of an indifference curve.

$u(4,0) = 16$, $u(0,4) = 16$, $u(2,2) = 8$. The average of two indifferent bundles is strictly worse, so convexity fails. Indifference curves are quarter-circles bowed away from the origin (concave to the origin); such a consumer specializes in one good at the optimum.

eDoes $u = \min\{x, y\}$ satisfy weak monotonicity? Strict monotonicity? Give a numerical bundle to support each answer.

Weak: yes — from $(3,3)$, moving to $(4,4)$ raises $u$ from 3 to 4 and more of both never lowers the min. Strict: no — from $(3,3)$ to $(4,3)$, $u$ stays at 3 even though $x$ rose and $y$ didn’t fall.

fWrite a utility function and state the MRS for each: (i) Liam only cares about total caffeine, and an espresso ($x$) has three times the caffeine of a tea ($y$). (ii) Mia eats two tacos ($x$) with every one drink ($y$) and cares only about complete meals.

(i) Perfect substitutes: $u = 3x + y$, $\text{MRS} = -3$ (he gives up 3 teas per espresso; straight-line curves).
(ii) Perfect complements with ideal ratio $x{:}y = 2{:}1$: $u = \min\{x, 2y\}$ (check $(2,1)$: $\min\{2,2\}$ ✓). Kink ray $x = 2y$; the MRS is undefined at the kink ($-\infty$ on the vertical arm, $0$ on the horizontal arm).

2

20 ptsCobb–Douglas with an endowment. Rosa has $U(x,y) = x^2 y$. Prices are $p_x$ and $p_y$. She enters the world with an endowment of $x = 6$ and $y = 4$.

aDerive Rosa’s MRS. Do her preferences exhibit diminishing MRS? Explain.

$MU_x = 2xy$, $MU_y = x^2$, so $\text{MRS} = -\dfrac{2xy}{x^2} = -\dfrac{2y}{x}$ (exponent ratio $\alpha/\beta = 2$ times $y/x$, with the minus sign for “give up $y$”). Moving right along a curve, $x$ rises and $y$ falls, so $|\text{MRS}| = 2y/x$ falls and the curve flattens → diminishing MRS. ✓

bAre these preferences homothetic? Explain using the MRS.

Yes. $\text{MRS}(tx, ty) = -\dfrac{2ty}{tx} = -\dfrac{2y}{x} = \text{MRS}(x,y)$: the MRS depends only on the ratio $y/x$, so it is constant along every ray from the origin.

cWrite Rosa’s budget constraint. What is special about the point $(6,4)$ on it?

$p_x x + p_y y = 6p_x + 4p_y$. Income is the market value of the endowment, so the line always passes through $(6,4)$ whatever the prices; price changes pivot the line around that point.

dDerive the Marshallian demand functions $x^*(p_x,p_y)$ and $y^*(p_x,p_y)$. (Tangency, then substitute into the budget.)

Tangency: $\text{MRS} = -\dfrac{p_x}{p_y} \Rightarrow -\dfrac{2y}{x} = -\dfrac{p_x}{p_y} \Rightarrow p_y y = \tfrac12 p_x x$. Budget: $p_x x + \tfrac12 p_x x = 6p_x + 4p_y \Rightarrow \tfrac32 p_x x = 6p_x + 4p_y$.

$$x^* = \frac{2(6p_x + 4p_y)}{3p_x} = 4 + \frac{8p_y}{3p_x},\qquad y^* = \frac{6p_x + 4p_y}{3p_y} = \frac{2p_x}{p_y} + \frac{4}{3}.$$

Shortcut: Cobb–Douglas spends the share $\alpha/(\alpha+\beta) = 2/3$ of income on $x$.

eNormalize $p_y = 1$, $p_x = p$. Write the demands as functions of $p$. At $p = 2$, what bundle does Rosa choose, and is she a net buyer or net seller of $x$? Verify the value of what she sells equals the value of what she buys.

$x^*(p) = 4 + \dfrac{8}{3p}$, $\ y^*(p) = 2p + \dfrac{4}{3}$. At $p = 2$: $x^* = 4 + \tfrac43 = \tfrac{16}{3} \approx 5.33$, $y^* = \tfrac{16}{3} \approx 5.33$. She holds $6$ of $x$ and wants $5.33$ → net seller of $x$ (sells $\tfrac23$), net buyer of $y$ (buys $\tfrac43$). Value check: $2 \cdot \tfrac23 = \tfrac43 = 1 \cdot \tfrac43$. ✓ Budget check: $2(\tfrac{16}{3}) + \tfrac{16}{3} = 16 = 12 + 4$. ✓

fAt what price $p$ does Rosa neither buy nor sell (autarky)? Relate that number to her MRS at the endowment.

$x^*(p) = 6 \Rightarrow \dfrac{8}{3p} = 2 \Rightarrow p = \dfrac{4}{3}$. And $\text{MRS}(6,4) = -\dfrac{2\cdot 4}{6} = -\dfrac43 = -p$: at the autarky price the budget line is tangent to the indifference curve through $\omega$. For $p < 4/3$ she buys $x$; for $p > 4/3$ (like $p=2$) she sells it.

3

18 ptsQuasilinear with an endowment. Theo has $U(x,y) = 2\sqrt{x} + y$. Normalize $p_y = 1$, $p_x = p$. His endowment is $x = 4$, $y = 6$.

aSketch the indifference map. What geometric feature is special to quasilinear preferences, and why?

Curves $y = c - 2\sqrt{x}$: every curve is the same shape shifted vertically. Because $\text{MRS} = -1/\sqrt{x}$ does not involve $y$, the slope at a given $x$ is identical on every curve.

bDerive the MRS. Are the preferences homothetic?

$MU_x = x^{-1/2}$, $MU_y = 1$ ⇒ $\text{MRS} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$. Not homothetic: $\text{MRS}(tx,ty) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{tx}} \ne -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ — the MRS changes along a ray.

cWrite the budget constraint in terms of $p$.

$p x + y = 4p + 6$.

dDerive the Marshallian demand for $x$. What is remarkable about it?

Tangency: $-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt x} = -p \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{1}{p^2}$. It does not depend on income or on the endowment at all — the quasilinear signature (valid as long as $y^* \ge 0$).

eDerive the demand for $y$ and state the condition for it to be an interior solution.

$y^* = 4p + 6 - p x^* = 4p + 6 - \dfrac{1}{p}$. Interior iff $y^* \ge 0$, i.e. $4p + 6 \ge 1/p$ (true for every $p \gtrsim 0.15$; at very low $p$ he would want more $x$ than he can afford and would spend everything on $x$).

fFind the bundle at $p = \tfrac14$ and at $p = 1$. In each case say whether Theo is a net buyer or net seller of $x$, and find the autarky price.

$p = \tfrac14$: $x^* = 16$, $y^* = 1 + 6 - 4 = 3$ → buys $12$ units of $x$, pays with $3$ units of $y$ ($12 \cdot \tfrac14 = 3$ ✓). Net buyer.
$p = 1$: $x^* = 1$, $y^* = 4 + 6 - 1 = 9$ → sells $3$ units of $x$ for $3$ units of $y$. Net seller.
Autarky: $1/p^2 = 4 \Rightarrow p = \tfrac12$, and indeed $\text{MRS}(4,6) = -1/\sqrt4 = -p$. ✓

4

22 ptsEdgeworth box: smooth vs linear. Alice: $U_A = x_A y_A$, endowment $e_A = (3, 0.5)$. Ben: $U_B = x_B + 2y_B$, endowment $e_B = (1, 3.5)$.

aGive the dimensions of the Edgeworth box and each person’s utility at the endowment.

$X = 3 + 1 = 4$, $Y = 0.5 + 3.5 = 4$: a $4 \times 4$ box. $U_A(\omega) = 3(0.5) = 1.5$; $U_B(\omega) = 1 + 2(3.5) = 8$.

bCompute each MRS at the endowment. Is the endowment Pareto optimal? Who should sell $x$ to whom, and at what range of prices (in $y$ per $x$)?

$\text{MRS}_A = -y_A/x_A = -0.5/3 = -1/6$; $\text{MRS}_B = -1/2$ (constant). Unequal ⇒ not PO. Ben values $x$ more ($|\text{MRS}_B| = \tfrac12$ units of $y$ per $x$ vs Alice’s $\tfrac16$), so Alice sells $x$ to Ben for $y$ at any rate between $1/6$ and $1/2$ units of $y$ per unit of $x$ — both gain.

cWrite Alice’s indifference curve through the endowment, and Ben’s indifference curve through the endowment in Alice’s coordinates.

Alice: $x_A y_A = 1.5$. Ben: $(4 - x_A) + 2(4 - y_A) = 8 \Rightarrow x_A + 2y_A = 4$, a straight line of slope $-\tfrac12$ through $(3, 0.5)$. Ben’s better-off side: Ben’s bundle grows as Alice’s shrinks, so $U_B \ge 8 \iff x_A + 2y_A \le 4$ — the side of the line toward $O_A$.

dFind where the two curves intersect and describe the lens of allocations that Pareto dominate the endowment.

Substitute $y_A = (4 - x_A)/2$ into $x_A y_A = 1.5$: $\tfrac12 x_A(4 - x_A) = 1.5 \Rightarrow x_A^2 - 4x_A + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow x_A = 1$ or $3$. Intersections $(1, 1.5)$ and $(3, 0.5)$ (the endowment itself). The lens is the region with $x_A y_A \ge 1.5$ and $x_A + 2y_A \le 4$, spanning $x_A \in [1, 3]$ — Alice ends up with less $x$ and more $y$ than at $\omega$.

eSolve for the contract curve and describe it in the box (be careful at the edges).

Interior tangency $\text{MRS}_A = \text{MRS}_B$: $-\dfrac{y_A}{x_A} = -\dfrac12 \Rightarrow y_A = \tfrac12 x_A$, a ray from $O_A$ that reaches the right edge at $(4, 2)$. From there the contract curve runs up the right edge $x_A = 4$, $y_A \in [2, 4]$, to $O_B$: Alice holds all the $x$, Ben holds only $y$, and no trade can help Ben without hurting Alice.

fIdentify the core: the Pareto-optimal allocations that Pareto dominate the endowment. Give the endpoints.

On $y_A = \tfrac12 x_A$: $U_A = \tfrac12 x_A^2 \ge 1.5 \Rightarrow x_A \ge \sqrt3 \approx 1.732$; $U_B = (4 - x_A) + 2(4 - \tfrac12 x_A) = 12 - 2x_A \ge 8 \Rightarrow x_A \le 2$. Core: $y_A = \tfrac12 x_A$ with $x_A \in [\sqrt3,\ 2]$, i.e. from $\approx(1.73, 0.87)$ to $(2, 1)$. Alice sells between $1$ and $1.27$ units of $x$ and receives between $0.37$ and $0.5$ units of $y$.

5

18 ptsPareto dominance with a Leontief consumer. Total endowment $E = (12, 6)$. Consumer 1: $u_1 = \min\{x_1, 2y_1\}$. Consumer 2: $u_2 = x_2 + y_2$. Allocations (consumer 1’s bundle first): $A = \{(4,4),(8,2)\}$, $B = \{(6,3),(6,3)\}$, $C = \{(4,2),(8,4)\}$.

aAre $A$, $B$, $C$ feasible? Explain.

Yes: in each, $x$ sums to $12$ ($4+8$, $6+6$, $4+8$) and $y$ sums to $6$ ($4+2$, $3+3$, $2+4$).

bCompute each consumer’s utility at each allocation. For consumer 1, say which good (if any) is idle.

$A$: $u_1 = \min\{4, 8\} = 4$ (only $2$ of the $4$ units of $y$ are used — $2$ idle), $u_2 = 10$.
$B$: $u_1 = \min\{6, 6\} = 6$ (balanced), $u_2 = 9$.
$C$: $u_1 = \min\{4, 4\} = 4$ (balanced), $u_2 = 12$.

cDoes $B$ Pareto dominate $A$? Does $A$ Pareto dominate $B$?

Neither. $A \to B$ raises $u_1$ ($4 \to 6$) but lowers $u_2$ ($10 \to 9$); $B \to A$ does the reverse. Pareto dominance requires nobody to be worse off.

dDoes $C$ Pareto dominate $A$? Explain the trade in words and why it hurts nobody.

Yes. Consumer 1 is exactly as well off ($4 \to 4$) and consumer 2 is strictly better off ($10 \to 12$). The move hands consumer 1’s two idle units of $y$ to consumer 2: consumer 1 needs $y$ only in the ratio $x = 2y$, so with $x_1 = 4$ any $y_1$ beyond $2$ adds nothing; consumer 2 values every unit.

eIs $A$ Pareto optimal? Is $C$? Justify each.

$A$: no — $C$ dominates it. $C$: yes — consumer 1 sits on the kink ray $x_1 = 2y_1$ with nothing idle, so taking any $x$ or $y$ from consumer 1 lowers the min, and consumer 2 (monotone) can only gain by taking something. In general the Pareto set here is the ray $x_1 = 2y_1$; since $E = (12,6)$ is itself in the $2{:}1$ ratio, that ray runs corner to corner.

fFind a feasible allocation that Pareto dominates $B$, or explain why none exists.

None exists: at $B$ consumer 1 is balanced ($6 = 2\cdot 3$, no idle units) and is on the Pareto set. Helping consumer 2 means taking $x$ or $y$ from consumer 1, which lowers $u_1$; helping consumer 1 means taking from consumer 2, which lowers $u_2$. $B$ is Pareto optimal.

B

Mock Test B

Five problems, 100 points, ~75 minutes. Different angles on the same skills as Mock A — do this one a few days later, closed-notes.

Coverage: P1 axioms, transformations & MRS tests • P2 perfect substitutes and perfect complements • P3 Pareto dominance with a quasilinear consumer • P4 Edgeworth box (Cobb–Douglas vs Cobb–Douglas) • P5 Edgeworth box (perfect substitutes both).

1

22 ptsAxioms and ordinal utility.

aDefine weak convexity of preferences in words and in symbols. What shape does it give indifference curves? Give an example of preferences that are weakly but not strictly convex.

Averages are at least as good as extremes: if $A \succsim C$ and $B \succsim C$ then $tA + (1-t)B \succsim C$ for all $t \in [0,1]$ (equivalently, the better-than set is convex). Curves bow toward the origin (or are straight). Perfect substitutes $u = ax + by$: straight-line curves, so the average of two indifferent bundles is exactly indifferent, never strictly better.

bExplain in two or three sentences why two indifference curves cannot cross. Name every axiom you use.

Suppose curves 1 and 2 cross at $A$. Choose $B$ on curve 1 and $C$ on curve 2 with $C$ containing more of both goods than $B$; by monotonicity $C \succ B$. But $A \sim B$ and $A \sim C$, so by transitivity $B \sim C$ — a contradiction. Hence the curves never cross.

cNadia’s utility is $u = \ln x + \ln y$. Show that $V = xy$ and $W = 5xy + 2$ represent the same preferences, and compute the MRS from each to confirm.

$V = e^{u}$ and $W = 5e^{u} + 2$; both are increasing functions of $u$ (positive monotonic transformations). MRS: $u$: $-\dfrac{1/x}{1/y} = -\dfrac{y}{x}$; $V$: $-\dfrac{y}{x}$; $W$: $-\dfrac{5y}{5x} = -\dfrac{y}{x}$. Identical MRS ⇒ identical indifference map.

dIs $u = x + y$ strictly monotone? Is $u = xy$ strictly monotone for $x, y > 0$? What happens to $u = xy$ on the axis $y = 0$?

$x + y$: yes, $MU_x = MU_y = 1 > 0$ everywhere. $xy$: on the interior $MU_x = y > 0$ and $MU_y = x > 0$, so yes. On $y = 0$, raising $x$ leaves $u = 0$, so strict monotonicity fails there (only weak holds) — which is why Cobb–Douglas curves never touch the axes.

eFor $u = \ln x + y$: derive the MRS, then decide (with justification) whether the preferences are homothetic and whether they exhibit diminishing MRS.

$MU_x = 1/x$, $MU_y = 1$ ⇒ $\text{MRS} = -\dfrac{1}{x}$. Not homothetic: $\text{MRS}(tx, ty) = -\dfrac{1}{tx} \ne -\dfrac{1}{x}$ — the slope changes as you move out along a ray (at $(1,1)$ it is $-1$, at $(2,2)$ it is $-\tfrac12$). Diminishing MRS: yes — moving right along any curve $x$ rises, so $|\text{MRS}| = 1/x$ falls and the curve flattens. (Quasilinear: the MRS has no $y$ in it, so every curve is a vertical shift of every other.)

fA classmate writes: “Allocation $B$ gives total utility $20$ while $A$ gives $18$, so $B$ Pareto dominates $A$.” Give two distinct reasons this is wrong.

(1) Utility is ordinal: each person’s $u$ can be rescaled by any increasing transformation, so a “total” across people is meaningless — no interpersonal comparisons. (2) Pareto dominance is person-by-person: $B$ dominates $A$ only if nobody is worse off and someone is better off. A higher total is consistent with one person being made worse off.

2

20 ptsPerfect substitutes and perfect complements. Part I. Jamal only cares about caffeine. A cold brew ($x$) has twice the caffeine of a drip coffee ($y$). Part II. Mei eats dumplings ($x$) only with sauce ($y$), exactly three dumplings per packet of sauce.

aWrite a utility function for Jamal and find his MRS. Describe his indifference map.

$U = 2x + y$ (any positive multiple works). $\text{MRS} = -2$: he always gives up exactly $2$ drips for $1$ cold brew. Curves are parallel straight lines with slope $-2$.

Shown with the budget from part (b): the curves are steeper than the budget line, so the optimum is the $x$-axis corner.

bWith $M = 30$, $p_x = 4$, $p_y = 3$, find Jamal’s demand. Use the bang-per-buck rule.

$\dfrac{MU_x}{p_x} = \dfrac{2}{4} = 0.5$ utils per dollar vs $\dfrac{MU_y}{p_y} = \dfrac{1}{3} \approx 0.33$ ⇒ cold brew gives more per dollar ⇒ corner: all income on $x$. $x^* = 30/4 = 7.5$, $y^* = 0$, $U = 15$.

cNow $p_x = 8$, $p_y = 3$. Find the demand. What if instead $p_x = 6$, $p_y = 3$?

$\dfrac{MU_x}{p_x} = \dfrac{2}{8} = 0.25 < \dfrac{MU_y}{p_y} = 0.33$ ⇒ all on $y$: $x^* = 0$, $y^* = 10$, $U = 10$. At $p_x = 6$: $\dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ exactly, the budget line coincides with an indifference curve: he is indifferent among every bundle with $6x + 3y = 30$ (demand is a whole segment).

dAll prices and income triple. What happens to Jamal’s demand, and what property is this?

Nothing changes: the budget set $3p_x x + 3p_y y \le 3M$ is the same set as $p_x x + p_y y \le M$. Demand is homogeneous of degree zero in $(p_x, p_y, M)$.

eWrite Mei’s utility function. With income $M$ and prices $p_x, p_y$, derive her demand functions.

Ideal ratio $x = 3y$, so $U = \min\{x, 3y\}$ (check: at $(3,1)$, $\min\{3,3\}$ — balanced). At the optimum she is at the kink: $x = 3y$. Budget: $p_x(3y) + p_y y = M \Rightarrow y^* = \dfrac{M}{3p_x + p_y}$, $x^* = \dfrac{3M}{3p_x + p_y}$. (E.g. $M=18, p_x=2, p_y=3$: $y^* = 2$, $x^* = 6$.)

fSuppose instead Mei has an endowment of $9$ dumplings and $1$ sauce packet, with $p_y = 1$ and $p_x = p$. Find her demands as functions of $p$, then evaluate at $p = 1$ and describe the trade.

Income $M = 9p + 1$. $y^* = \dfrac{9p + 1}{3p + 1}$, $x^* = \dfrac{3(9p+1)}{3p+1}$. At $p = 1$: $y^* = 2.5$, $x^* = 7.5$. At the endowment $U = \min\{9, 3\} = 3$ with $6$ idle dumplings; she sells $1.5$ dumplings for $1.5$ packets and reaches $U = \min\{7.5, 7.5\} = 7.5$. Value check: $1.5 \cdot 1 = 1.5 \cdot 1$. ✓

3

18 ptsPareto dominance with a quasilinear consumer. Total endowment $E = (9, 12)$. Consumer 1: $u_1 = 2\sqrt{x_1} + y_1$. Consumer 2: $u_2 = x_2 + y_2$. Allocation $A = \{(4, 6), (5, 6)\}$.

aIs $A$ feasible? Compute both utilities at $A$.

$4 + 5 = 9$ and $6 + 6 = 12$ → feasible. $u_1 = 2\sqrt4 + 6 = 10$; $u_2 = 5 + 6 = 11$.

bConsider $B = \{(1, 8.5), (8, 3.5)\}$. Is it feasible? Compute both utilities.

$1 + 8 = 9$, $8.5 + 3.5 = 12$ → feasible. $u_1 = 2\sqrt1 + 8.5 = 10.5$; $u_2 = 8 + 3.5 = 11.5$.

cDoes $B$ Pareto dominate $A$? Explain using the definition.

Yes: $u_1$ rises $10 \to 10.5$ and $u_2$ rises $11 \to 11.5$. Both are strictly better off (so $B$ strictly Pareto dominates $A$).

dDescribe the trade from $A$ to $B$: who gives up which good, and how much? Use each consumer’s MRS at $A$ to explain why both gain.

Consumer 1 gives up $3$ units of $x$ and receives $2.5$ units of $y$; consumer 2 does the reverse. At $A$, $\text{MRS}_1 = -1/\sqrt{x_1} = -1/\sqrt4 = -0.5$: consumer 1 will part with an $x$ for as little as $0.5$ of $y$. $\text{MRS}_2 = -1$: consumer 2 will pay up to $1$ unit of $y$ per $x$. The trade’s rate, $2.5/3 \approx 0.83$ units of $y$ per $x$, lies strictly between $0.5$ and $1$, so both gain.

eWrite the condition for an interior allocation to be Pareto optimal in this economy and solve it. Is $B$ Pareto optimal? Describe the contract curve.

$\text{MRS}_1 = \text{MRS}_2 \Rightarrow -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x_1}} = -1 \Rightarrow x_1 = 1$, for any $y_1 \in [0, 12]$. $B$ has $x_1 = 1$, so it is Pareto optimal. The contract curve is the vertical line $x_1 = 1$ in the box — consumer 1’s MRS depends only on $x_1$ (quasilinear), so once $x_1$ is right, $y$ can be split any way.

fFind a different feasible allocation that also Pareto dominates $A$ and is Pareto optimal.

Any point on $x_1 = 1$ inside the lens, e.g. $\{(1, 9), (8, 3)\}$: $u_1 = 2 + 9 = 11 > 10$, $u_2 = 8 + 3 = 11 \ge 11$. On the line $x_1 = 1$, the lens is $u_1 = 2 + y_1 \ge 10 \Rightarrow y_1 \ge 8$ and $u_2 = 8 + (12 - y_1) \ge 11 \Rightarrow y_1 \le 9$; so the core is $x_1 = 1$, $y_1 \in [8, 9]$.

4

22 ptsEdgeworth box: Cobb–Douglas vs Cobb–Douglas. Ana: $U_A = x_A y_A$, endowment $e_A = (2, 6)$. Bo: $U_B = x_B y_B^2$, endowment $e_B = (6, 2)$.

aBox dimensions and each utility at the endowment.

$X = Y = 8$. $U_A(\omega) = 2 \cdot 6 = 12$; $U_B(\omega) = 6 \cdot 2^2 = 24$.

bDerive each person’s MRS in their own variables.

$\text{MRS}_A = -\dfrac{y_A}{x_A}$ ($\alpha/\beta = 1$). $\text{MRS}_B = -\dfrac{y_B^2}{2x_By_B} = -\dfrac{y_B}{2x_B}$ ($\alpha/\beta = 1/2$).

cEvaluate both at the endowment. Who buys $x$ from whom, and in what price range (in $y$ per $x$)?

$\text{MRS}_A(\omega) = -6/2 = -3$; $\text{MRS}_B(\omega) = -2/(2\cdot6) = -1/6$. Ana values $x$ far more ($|\text{MRS}_A| = 3 > 1/6$), so Ana buys $x$ from Bo, paying in $y$, at any rate between $1/6$ and $3$ units of $y$ per unit of $x$. The endowment is not PO.

dSolve for the contract curve in Ana’s coordinates. Check it passes through both origins, and confirm with the general Cobb–Douglas formula.

$\text{MRS}_A = \text{MRS}_B$ (minus signs cancel): $\dfrac{y_A}{x_A} = \dfrac{8 - y_A}{2(8 - x_A)} \Rightarrow 2y_A(8 - x_A) = x_A(8 - y_A) \Rightarrow 16y_A - 2x_Ay_A = 8x_A - x_Ay_A \Rightarrow 16y_A - x_Ay_A = 8x_A$

$$y_A = \frac{8x_A}{16 - x_A}.$$

$x_A = 0 \Rightarrow 0$ ✓; $x_A = 8 \Rightarrow 64/8 = 8$ ✓. General formula with $r_A = 1$, $r_B = \tfrac12$, $X = Y = 8$: $y_A = \dfrac{\tfrac12 \cdot 8\, x_A}{8 - \tfrac12 x_A} = \dfrac{4x_A}{8 - x_A/2} = \dfrac{8x_A}{16 - x_A}$. ✓

eDoes the contract curve lie above or below the diagonal? Explain economically.

At $x_A = 4$: $y_A = 32/12 \approx 2.67 < 4$ → below the diagonal. Ana’s relative taste for $x$ ($r_A = 1$) exceeds Bo’s ($r_B = 1/2$; Bo leans toward $y$), so efficient allocations give Ana relatively more $x$ than $y$ and Bo relatively more $y$.

fFind the endpoint of the core on Ana’s side: the point on the contract curve where $U_A = U_A(\omega)$. (The other endpoint, where $U_B = 24$, is $x_A \approx 5.87$ — take it as given.) State the core.

$x_A \cdot \dfrac{8x_A}{16 - x_A} = 12 \Rightarrow 8x_A^2 = 192 - 12x_A \Rightarrow 2x_A^2 + 3x_A - 48 = 0 \Rightarrow x_A = \dfrac{-3 + \sqrt{9 + 384}}{4} = \dfrac{-3 + \sqrt{393}}{4} \approx 4.21$, with $y_A \approx 2.85$. Core: the contract-curve segment $x_A \in [4.21,\ 5.87]$, i.e. from $\approx(4.21, 2.85)$ to $\approx(5.87, 4.64)$. Ana ends up buying between $2.2$ and $3.9$ units of $x$ and giving up between $1.4$ and $3.2$ units of $y$.

5

18 ptsEdgeworth box: perfect substitutes both. Orange juice ($x$) and apple juice ($y$). Person 1 regards one glass of orange as equivalent to three glasses of apple; Person 2 regards one glass of apple as equivalent to three glasses of orange. Each starts with two glasses of each juice.

aWrite utility functions $U_1(x_1,y_1)$ and $U_2(x_2,y_2)$.

$U_1 = 3x_1 + y_1$ (one orange is worth three apples). $U_2 = x_2 + 3y_2$ (one apple is worth three oranges).

bState each MRS. Who values orange juice more? What are the box dimensions and the utilities at the endowment?

$\text{MRS}_1 = -3$, $\text{MRS}_2 = -1/3$ (apples given up per orange). Person 1 values orange ($x$) nine times as much, relatively. Box $4 \times 4$; $U_1(\omega) = 3(2) + 2 = 8$, $U_2(\omega) = 2 + 3(2) = 8$.

cWrite both indifference curves through the endowment in Person 1’s coordinates and describe the lens.

Person 1: $3x_1 + y_1 = 8$ (slope $-3$). Person 2: $(4 - x_1) + 3(4 - y_1) = 8 \Rightarrow x_1 + 3y_1 = 8$ (slope $-1/3$). Lens: $3x_1 + y_1 \ge 8$ and $x_1 + 3y_1 \le 8$ — the wedge to the lower-right of $\omega$, where Person 1 has more orange and less apple.

dFind the set of Pareto-optimal allocations and explain why any allocation off that set can be improved.

Whenever Person 1 still holds some apple ($y_1 > 0$) and Person 2 still holds some orange ($x_2 > 0$, i.e. $x_1 < 4$), they can swap orange for apple at any rate between $1/3$ and $3$ apples per orange (between the two $|\text{MRS}|$s) and both gain. So PO requires $y_1 = 0$ or $x_1 = 4$: the Pareto set is the bottom edge of the box plus the right edge (an L from $O_1$ along the bottom to the corner $(4,0)$, then up to $O_2$).

eIdentify the core.

Bottom edge ($y_1 = 0$): $U_1 = 3x_1 \ge 8 \Rightarrow x_1 \ge 8/3$; $U_2 = (4 - x_1) + 12 \ge 8$ always. Right edge ($x_1 = 4$): $U_1 = 12 + y_1 \ge 8$ always; $U_2 = 3(4 - y_1) \ge 8 \Rightarrow y_1 \le 4/3$. Core: $\{(x_1, 0): 8/3 \le x_1 \le 4\} \cup \{(4, y_1): 0 \le y_1 \le 4/3\}$. The corner $(4,0)$ — Person 1 holds all the orange, Person 2 all the apple — gives $U_1 = U_2 = 12$.

fSuppose instead Person 2 also had $U_2 = 3x_2 + y_2$. What is the Pareto set now? Will any trade occur?

Identical constant MRS ($-3 = -3$) at every allocation, so no mutually beneficial trade ever exists: every allocation in the box is Pareto optimal (the Pareto set is the whole box) and there is no reason to trade away from $\omega$.
